{{Short description|Type of filtration in the theory of stochastic processes}}
In the theory of [[stochastic processes]] in [[mathematics]] and [[statistics]], the '''generated filtration''' or '''natural filtration'''  associated to a stochastic process is a [[filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] associated to the process which records its "past behaviour" at each time. It is in a sense the simplest filtration available for studying the given process: all information concerning the process, and only that information, is available in the natural filtration.

==Formal definition==
Let 
*<math> (\Omega, \mathcal A, P) </math> be a [[probability space]].

*<math>(I, \le)</math> be a [[total order|totally ordered]] [[index set]]. In many examples, the index set <math>I</math> is the [[natural numbers]] <math>\N</math> (possibly including 0) or an [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] <math>[0, T]</math> or <math>[0, +\infty).</math> 

*<math>(S, \Sigma)</math> be a [[measurable space]]. Often, the state space <math>S</math> is often the [[real line]] <math>\R</math> or [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n.</math> 

*<math>X:I\times\Omega\to S</math> be a [[stochastic process]].

Then the '''natural filtration of''' <math>\mathcal{A}</math> '''with respect to''' <math>X</math> is defined to be the filtration <math>\mathbb{F}^X=\mathcal{F}^X_\bullet=(\mathcal{F}^X_i)_{i\in I}</math> given by

:<math>\mathcal{F}^X_i = \sigma \left\{ \left. X_{j}^{-1} (B) \right| j \in I, j \leq i, B \in \Sigma \right\},</math>

i.e., the smallest [[sigma algebra|''&sigma;''-algebra]] on <math>\Omega</math> that contains all pre-images of <math>\Sigma</math>-measurable subsets of <math>S</math> for "times" <math>j</math> up to <math>i</math>.

Any stochastic process <math>X</math> is an [[adapted process]] with respect to its natural filtration.

==Examples==
Two examples are given below, the [[Bernoulli process]] and the [[Wiener process]]. The simpler example, the Bernoullii process, is treated somewhat awkwardly and verbosely, belabored, but using a notation that allows more direct contact with the Wiener process.

===Bernoulli process===
The [[Bernoulli process]] is the process <math>X</math> of coin-flips. The sample space is <math>\Omega=\{0,1\}^\N=2^\N,</math> the set of all infinitely-long sequences of binary strings. A single point <math>\omega\in\Omega</math> then specifies a single, specific infinitely long sequence. The index set <math>I=\N</math> is the natural numbers. The state space is the set of symbols <math>S=\{H,T\}</math> indicating heads or tails. Fixing <math>\omega</math> to a specific sequence, <math>X(i,\omega)</math> then indicates the <math>i</math>'th outcome of the coin-flip, heads or tails. The conventional notation for this process is <math>X_i=X(i,-),</math> indicating that all possibilities should be considered at time <math>i.</math>  

The sigma algebra on the state space contains four elements: <math>\Sigma=\{\varnothing,\{H\},\{T\},S\}.</math> The set <math>X_{j}^{-1}(B)</math> for some <math>B\in\Sigma</math> is then a [[cylinder set]], consisting of all strings having an element of <math>B</math> at location <math>j:</math>

:<math>X_{j}^{-1}(B) = \{\omega\in\Omega : X(j,\omega)=b \text{ and } b\in B\}</math>

The filtration is then the sigma algebra generated by these cylinder sets; it is exactly as above:
:<math>\mathcal{F}_i = \sigma \left\{ X_{j}^{-1} (B) : j \leq i, B \in \Sigma \right\},</math>

The sub-sigma-algebra <math>\mathcal{F}_i</math> can be understood as the sigma algebra for which the first <math>i</math> symbols of the process have been fixed, and all the remaining symbols are left indeterminate.

This can also be looked at from a "sideways" direction. The set
:<math>C(i,\omega)=\{\alpha\in\Omega: X(j,\alpha)=X(j,\omega) \text{ for } j\le i\}</math>
is a cylinder set, for which all points <math>\alpha\in C(i,\omega)</math> match exactly <math>X(-,\omega)</math> for the first <math>i</math> coin-flips. Clearly, one has that <math>C(k,\omega)\subset C(i,\omega)</math> whenever <math>k>i.</math> That is, as more and more of the initial sequence is fixed, the corresponding cylinder sets become finer.

Let <math>A\in\mathcal{A}</math> be one of the sets in the sigma algebra <math>\mathcal{A}.</math> Cylinder sets can be defined in a corresponding manner:
:<math>C(i,A)=\{\alpha\in\Omega: X(j,\alpha)=X(j,\omega) \text{ for } j\le i \text{ and } \omega\in A\}</math>
Again, one has that <math>C(k,A)\subset C(i,A)</math> whenever <math>k>i.</math>

The filtration can be understood to be
:<math>\mathcal{F}_i = \{C(i,A) | A\in \mathcal{A} \}</math>
consisting of all sets for which the first <math>i</math> outcomes have been fixed. As time progresses, the filtrations become  finer, so that <math>\mathcal{F}_i \subset \mathcal{F}_k</math> for <math>i<k.</math>

===Wiener process===
The [[Wiener process]] <math>X</math> can be taken to be set in the [[classical Wiener space]] <math>\Omega = C_0([0,T])</math> consisting of all continuous functions on the interval <math>I=[0,T].</math> The state space <math>S</math> can be taken to be Euclidean space: <math>S=\R^n</math> and <math>\Sigma=\mathcal{B}(\R^n)</math> the standard [[Borel algebra]] on <math>\R^n.</math> The Wiener process is then <math>X:I\times\Omega\to S.</math>

The interpretation is that fixing a single point <math>\omega\in\Omega</math> fixes a single continuous path <math>X(\cdot,\omega):I\to S.</math> Unlike the Bernoulli process, however, it is not possible to construct the filtration out of the components 
:<math>X_t^{-1}(B) = \{\omega\in\Omega : X(t,\omega)=x \text{ and } x\in B\}</math>
for some <math>B\in\mathcal{B}(\R^n).</math> The primary issue is that <math>I</math> is uncountable, and so one cannot perform a naive union of such sets, while also preserving continuity. However, the approach of fixing the initial portion of the path does follow through. By analogy, define
:<math>C(t,\omega)=\{\alpha\in\Omega: X(s,\alpha)=X(s,\omega) \text{ for } s\le t\}</math>
This consists of all continuous functions, that is, elements of <math>\Omega</math> for which the initial segment <math>s\le t</math> exactly matches a selected sample function <math>X(\cdot,\omega).</math>  As before, one has that <math>C(u,\omega)\subset C(t,\omega)</math> whenever <math>t<u,</math> that is, the set becomes strictly finer as time increases.

Presuming that one has defined a sigma algebra <math>\mathcal{A}</math> on the (classical) Wiener space, then for a given <math>A\in\mathcal{A},</math> the corresponding cylinder can be defined as
:<math>C(t,A)=\{\alpha\in\Omega: X(s,\alpha)=X(s,\omega) \text{ for } s\le t \text{ and } \omega\in A\}</math>
which also becomes finer for increasing time: <math>C(u,A)\subset C(t,A)</math> whenever <math>t<u.</math>

The desired filtration is then
:<math>\mathcal{F}_t = \{C(t,A) | A\in \mathcal{A} \}.</math>
As before, it becomes strictly finer with increasing time: <math>\mathcal{F}_t \subset \mathcal{F}_u</math> whenever <math>t<u.</math>
